thread.title: This credit-card company is teaching America how to do tax reform right

author: Tim Mullaney
title: This credit-card company is teaching America how to do tax reform right
text:
Oh, the irony: A benighted Congress passes a spendthrift, deficit-financed tax cut aimed at corporations and the 1%. 
A clueless White House hails companies that offer gimmicky $1,000-per-employee bonuses paid for with tax-cut proceeds, citing them as evidence that an already healthy economy is shaking off a torpor that exists only in President Donald Trump’s head.
And the one company that exploits the tax bill to promote investment and fiscal responsibility by its employees is a credit-card company?
Giggle if you like, but Visa’s plan to boost its 401(k) match is maybe the best news to come out of the tax bill. The company said Monday that it will boost its maximum match to 5% of a worker’s income from 3%. And that money gets invested, rather than spent.
Visa’s move may be the only real investment spurred by the tax bill, which is mostly a series of giveways to middling-wealthy business owners. And, yes, it comes after those benighted congressional Republicans flirted with slashing the amount workers can contribute to 401(k)s on a tax-deferred basis before political pressure from Trump’s Twitter feed helped back them down . 
My MarketWatch colleague Maria Lamagna has already run the numbers . Instead of contributing a maximum of 3% of base pay, or $3,000 for a $100,000 a year middle-manager annually, Visa will bump that to 5% — still not especially generous, since many companies top out their contributions at 6% — but other parts of Visa’s plan are above the norm. Best guess at how much that will cost — Visa didn’t respond to an interview request — is no more than $25 million a year, since Visa’s 10-k form said it spent $58 million on 401(k) expenses in fiscal 2017.
For most workers, an extra $750 to $2,000 (depending on their income) tax-deferred each year is worth a whole lot more than the taxable, flat $1,000 one-time bonuses that companies from AT&T to Southwest Airlines and Wells Fargo are doling out to their employees. The only catch is that you generally have to wait until you’re 59½ to enjoy it without tax penalties. 
Read: This is how you can withdraw from your 401(k) at 55 — without paying a penalty 
What does $1,000 buy, if you’re not Gary Cohn, the White House adviser who thought middle-class families would buy cars or kitchen with tax cuts that were a fraction of what those items cost?
Well, a new iPhone. Or two airplane tickets in coach from New York to Los Angeles, if you’ve got a place to stay. Or a Starbucks run on most work days for a year. For many people, a $650 after-tax bonus (don’t forget state taxes) means part of a mortgage payment or a better Christmas. 
You know what it’s not?
It’s not a raise.
Economically, a bonus is useful when the economy is sluggish and needs a jolt of fresh consumer spending at the margin — which is pretty much the opposite of what is happening now. Consumer spending rose 2.6% in last 12 months, healthy by recent standards. Profit growth at the consumer-y companies in the Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA, +0.46% are healthy, from McDonalds MCD, -0.26% to Apple AAPL, -0.01% and, not least Visa V, -0.23% whose shares are up 46% in the last year. 
Read: Here’s what all 30 companies that make up the Dow industrials think about the tax cuts 
What the expansion has been lacking all along is investment, and the tax bill didn’t really do much to encourage it. Outside, perhaps, of the real estate industry the president came from. Scott Greenberg of the conservative Tax Foundation said on Twitter that the bill has so many new loopholes for real estate that the industry will operate virtually under its own tax code .
The bulk of the $1.4 trillion tax cut will be spent to cut rates on corporate income, and from most evidence corporations will mostly pay for stock buybacks rather than capital expenditures with their savings. Then there’s the cut for the business owners, which again is making it more attractive to take money out of the business, rather than leave it in.
Read: Tim Mullaney on the four worst things about the tax bill 
So if Visa wants to dangle a carrot that leads its employees to invest more, that’s a pretty unreservedly good thing. It’s easy, of course, to exaggerate the good this can do — as commenters on Maria’s piece argued, the first thing money invested in the stock market does is raise stock prices, which are already rather high. ( I’ve covered this recently here , and the numbers haven’t changed much).
But if you don’t believe that the stock market finances innovation, directly or not, you don’t believe in capitalism. How direct or indirectly that finds its way into new machines and software that make companies more profitable is up to the market, a task that over time it performs well even with some periods of overvaluation and some misallocated capital.
Boosting 401(k)s is a permanent investment in, mostly, America, rather than an invitation to consume more. That’s the simplest, best reason to prefer Visa’s plan to what other companies are doing.
